title: Finding a missing number in addition
keyIdea: A take-away can be turned into an add-on question. 10 − 8 = ? asks the same thing as 8 + ? = 10: what do I add to 8 to make 10? So you can use adding to subtract. Start on the smaller number and count up to the bigger one, or use an adding fact you already know: 6 + 4 = 10 tells you 10 − 6 = 4 and 10 − 4 = 6.

kid: A bus has 10 seats. 8 kids are on. How many more can get on? Count up from 8: 9, 10. That is 2 more. So 8 + 2 = 10.
Now think of it the other way. 10 seats, and 8 are taken. 10 take away 8 is 2. It is the same 2. 10 − 8 and 8 + ? = 10 ask the same thing.
When the two numbers are close, count up. For 12 − 9, start on 9 and hop: 10, 11, 12. Count the hops, not the start. That is 3 hops, so 12 − 9 = 3.
Facts you know help too. If you know 7 + 5 = 12, then you know 12 − 7 = 5. The box in 9 = 4 + □ is the part that is missing: 5.
adult: This is subtraction as an unknown addend. The US Common Core puts it in Grade 1 (1.OA.4, 'understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem', for example 'subtract 10 − 8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8'), and 1.OA.8 asks children to find the unknown in equations such as 8 + ? = 11 and 5 = □ − 3. The English national curriculum asks Year 1 pupils to 'solve missing number problems such as 7 = □ − 9' and to use related subtraction facts within 20.

The big idea is the part–whole relationship: two parts make a whole, so if you know the whole and one part, the missing part is the whole minus the known part. That is why one addition fact (6 + 4 = 10) gives a fact family of two subtractions (10 − 6 = 4, 10 − 4 = 6). Counting up from the smaller number to the larger one, often called finding the difference, is far quicker than counting back when the numbers are close: 15 − 13 is 2 hops up rather than 13 hops back.

Common mistakes to watch for: adding the two numbers you can see (writing 18 for 8 + □ = 10); giving back the known part or the whole instead of the missing part; counting the start number as a hop, so 12 − 9 comes out as 4; and reading the equals sign as 'the answer comes next', so 9 = 4 + □ gets 13. Say '= means is the same as' and check by putting the answer back in the gap.

In the lab your child fills empty seats on a bus and sees both number sentences, matches each take-away to the add-on question that asks the same thing, hops a frog up a number track and counts the hops, uses a known fact to answer a take-away, and fills the box on a balance until both sides are level.

familyTip: At snack time, line up 10 grapes in two rows of five and eat some while your child looks away. Ask, 'How many did I eat?' Let them count up from what is left to 10. Then say the take-away out loud together: '10 take away 7 is 3.' Try it with 9 or 12 grapes too.

visual.caption: Is the missing part 2 or 3? Count up from the small number. Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

practice.prompt: {a} + □ = 10. What number goes in the box?
practice.hint: Start on {a} and count up to 10. Count the hops.
practice.explain: {a} and {=10-a} make 10, so the box is {=10-a}. That also means 10 − {a} = {=10-a}.

practice.hint: Put your finger on {a} on a number track and hop up to {b}. How many hops?
practice.explain: From {a} up to {b} is {=b-a} hops, so {b} − {a} = {=b-a}.

practice.prompt: Which question asks the same thing as 10 − 7?
practice.hint: 10 − 7 asks: what do I add to 7 to get back to 10?
practice.explain: 7 + □ = 10 asks what joins 7 to make 10. The answer is 3 for both: 10 − 7 = 3.

practice.hint: = means 'is the same as'. 4 and what make 9?
practice.explain: 4 and 5 make 9, so both sides are the same: 9 = 4 + 5. 13 comes from adding 9 and 4, which is not the question.

pool.prompt: A bus has 10 seats. {a} children are on it. How many more can get on?
pool.hint: Count up from {a} to 10, or think {a} + ? = 10.

pool.prompt: □ + {a} = {b}. What number goes in the box?
pool.hint: The box is the missing part. Count up from {a} to {b}.
pool.explain: {=b-a} and {a} make {b}, so the box is {=b-a}.

pool.hint: 6 and 4 make 10. Take the 6 away. Which part is left?
pool.explain: 6 + 4 = 10, so taking 6 from 10 leaves the other part: 10 − 6 = 4.

pool.prompt: Ali works out 12 − 9 by counting up: 9, 10, 11, 12. He says 4. What went wrong?
pool.hint: Count only the hops: 9 to 10, 10 to 11, 11 to 12.
pool.explain: He counted the start number. There are 3 hops, so 12 − 9 = 3.

pool.prompt: Which is the quick way to do 15 − 13?
pool.hint: The two numbers are close together.
pool.explain: 13 to 15 is only 2 hops, so 15 − 13 = 2. Counting back 13 hops gets there too, but takes much longer.

pool.prompt: Sam says 8 + □ = 10 has 18 in the box. Is he right?
pool.hint: Put his answer back: is 8 + 18 the same as 10?
pool.explain: 8 + 18 is far more than 10. The box is 2, because 8 + 2 = 10.

pool.hint: Take one part away from the whole, 12. What part is left?
pool.explain: 12 is the whole and 7 and 5 are the parts. Take away 5 and 7 is left: 12 − 5 = 7.

pool.prompt: There are 9 apples in a box that holds 12. How many more fit?
pool.hint: Count up from 9 to 12 and count the hops.
pool.explain: 9, then 10, 11, 12: 3 hops. 9 + 3 = 12, so 3 more apples fit.
